questions.q: Merge: 'She heard the news. She fainted.'
questions.a: 'Hearing the news, she fainted' — participle merge on shared subject. A wrong answer 'She heard the news and she fainted' is grammatically legal but misses the tested device.

questions.q: Fix: 'Walking down the road, a snake appeared.'
questions.a: Dangling participle — 'walking' implies the snake walked. Fix: 'Walking down the road, I saw a snake' or 'As I walked down the road, a snake appeared.'

questions.q: Merge with an appositive: 'Mr Verma is our new principal. He introduced himself today.'
questions.a: 'Mr Verma, our new principal, introduced himself today.' A wrong answer 'Mr Verma who is our new principal' works but the appositive is the tighter, tested form.

questions.q: What common mix-up does this lesson flag about Synthesis merges separate sentences into one?
questions.a: Students simply stack sentences with 'and…and…and' or create dangling participles — 'Walking down the road, the house appeared' (the house wasn't walking).

questions.q: What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student combines 2-3 simple sentences into one grammatical sentence choosing the appropriate merging device, without dropping or distorting any idea.
